candidate.answerReason: The row and column restrictions force the positions of each color in turn. The resulting placement satisfies every restriction and is unique.

methods.label: Force one color at a time
methods.explanation:
Start with yellow, since its five pegs must occupy five different rows. There are exactly five rows, so every row must contain one yellow peg.

The single hole in the top row must therefore be yellow. In the second row, the first hole cannot be yellow because it is in the same column as the top yellow peg. Thus the second hole is yellow. In the third row, the first two columns already contain yellow pegs, so its yellow peg must occupy the third hole. Continuing this reasoning forces yellow into the rightmost hole of every row.

Set those yellow holes aside. The remaining holes form a smaller triangle with rows of lengths \(1,2,3,4\). The four red pegs must occupy different rows of this triangle, so the same reasoning forces red into its rightmost holes. Repeating with green, blue, and orange forces all the remaining positions.

Writing each row from left to right, the result is
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\text{yellow}\\
\text{red, yellow}\\
\text{green, red, yellow}\\
\text{blue, green, red, yellow}\\
\text{orange, blue, green, red, yellow}.
\end{array}
\]
Every row and every vertical column has distinct colors, and the color totals are correct. Thus this forced arrangement exists, and every valid arrangement must be this one. There is exactly \(\boxed{1}\) placement, choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: The proof uses elementary row and column restrictions and repeated forced choices, without formal graph theory or permutation formulas.
